justice: Spatial resources are dominated by a wide vehicular carriageway and open dirt parking/storage areas, while no formal sidewalk is visible on either side.
Accessibility is limited because the road edge is uneven and broken, with rocks, dirt shoulders, and no curb ramps or barrier-free pedestrian path.
Fairness across user groups is weak because cyclists and pedestrians appear to share the same deteriorated roadway without dedicated facilities or protective separation.
safety: The concrete road surface shows cracks, patches, and irregular edges, which can create conflict and loss-of-control risks for all users.
There are no visible crosswalks, speed-calming devices, lane markings, or protected pedestrian space along this segment.
Numerous low and crossing overhead utility wires and roadside utility poles create a visually cluttered environment and suggest weak infrastructure management.
Parked trucks and cars near the tree line and dirt shoulder may reduce sightlines and create roadside friction for drivers and cyclists.
livability: The street lacks visible shops, active frontages, seating, or community amenities, so it offers little support for daily social life.
Large vacant or undeveloped plots and temporary-looking site structures make the area feel transitional rather than neighborhood-serving.
Very few people are visible, indicating limited street activity and low social vitality.
The environment appears oriented to access and parking rather than to public life or everyday pedestrian use.
sustainability: Mature roadside trees provide some ecological value and partial shade, which is a positive green element.
However, the street design prioritizes mixed motor access and informal parking, with no visible bus stop, bike lane, or other clear low-carbon transport infrastructure.
Unpaved shoulders and exposed soil can contribute to dust and runoff problems, and no rain-garden or permeable drainage feature is evident.
The overhead wire-heavy infrastructure and scattered roadside condition suggest low-quality long-term environmental management.
aesthetics: Large mature trees add greenery and soften parts of the corridor, improving visual quality somewhat.
At the same time, the scene is dominated by overhead cables, utility poles, rough shoulders, and patched pavement, which reduce visual coherence.
Temporary-looking site cabins, open dirt lots, and scattered rocks create a utilitarian and unfinished appearance.
There is little architectural frontage, public art, or coordinated streetscape design to create a strong sense of place.
comfort: Tree canopy on the right and ahead offers limited thermal relief, but most of the roadway and roadside space remain exposed to sun.
Physical comfort is poor because there is no clear sidewalk, the road surface is uneven, and the shoulders are rough dirt with debris and stones.
Psychological comfort is reduced by the isolated feel of the street, with few people, little active frontage, and weak spatial definition.
There are no visible benches, shelters, or designated resting points for people spending time outdoors.
walkability: Walkability is very low because no continuous sidewalk or pedestrian track is visible along either side of the road.
The road edge is interrupted by dirt, rocks, utility poles, and uneven surfaces, making walking routes indirect and uncomfortable.
There are no marked crossings, curb extensions, pedestrian signs, or other facilities that support safe on-foot movement.
The sparse frontage activity and open undeveloped edges make the route less attractive and less legible for everyday walking.
bikeability: Bikeability is poor because there is no dedicated bike lane, shoulder marking, or protected cycling space on the corridor.
Cyclists would need to ride on a cracked, patched concrete roadway while also interacting with cars and parked vehicles.
The uneven road edge and dirt shoulders reduce maneuvering space and make it difficult to recover safely if forced aside.
No bicycle parking, bike wayfinding, or intersection treatments are visible to support cycling as a regular mode.
